subtype: Looking at the phone versus at the person [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Saurabh, and there was a day last spring when I nearly lost a friendship over a phone. I was telling my colleague Chetan about a difficult call with a supplier, a subject I had been carrying for days, and I noticed his eyes going down to his phone. Twice. My chest went tight. I thought, He doesn't care. I stopped mid-sentence and said, "You seem busy." Chetan looked up, embarrassed. "My sister's in surgery. I've been checking for news. I should've said." I felt terrible. We stopped, he put the phone face down on the table, and I finished my story. Now I say, "Do you need to check something? I can wait." It changes the whole conversation.

qa.q: What did Saurabh's colleague keep looking at?
qa.a: Chetan kept looking down at his phone.

qa.q: What did Saurabh feel when Chetan looked at his phone, and what was the real reason?
qa.a: Saurabh felt hurt, thinking Chetan didn't care, but Chetan was checking for news because his sister was in surgery.

qa.q: What could Saurabh do the next time a colleague glances at a phone during a talk?
qa.a: Saurabh could ask kindly whether they need to check something and offer to wait, instead of assuming disrespect.

qa.q: How might Chetan have felt when Saurabh stopped mid-sentence?
qa.a: Chetan felt embarrassed and probably worried, since he had been keeping his sister's surgery to himself.

grounding: Saurabh learns that a colleague's glance at a phone had a real reason and now asks rather than assumes.

subtype: Looking at the phone versus at the person [Interpreting]
passage: Supervisor's note. During Tuesday's planning meeting I noticed Chaitanya looking down at his phone while Pradeep was presenting the delivery figures. Pradeep's voice went flat, and he began to rush. At the end I asked both of them to stay. Pradeep said he felt Chaitanya wasn't listening. Chaitanya explained that the vendor had messaged about a delayed shipment and he'd been trying to reply. He was sorry that it had looked like boredom. I suggested a simple habit: if something urgent may interrupt, say so at the start, or ask for a moment. Pradeep said he'd also try asking, "Do you have a minute for full attention?" I will watch at the next meeting whether it helps.

qa.q: Which meeting did the supervisor describe?
qa.a: The supervisor described Tuesday's planning meeting.

qa.q: What did Pradeep feel about Chaitanya's phone, and what was Chaitanya actually doing?
qa.a: Pradeep felt ignored, sure Chaitanya wasn't listening, as his flat voice and rushing suggest, but Chaitanya was replying to a vendor about a delayed shipment.

qa.q: What simple habit could help them in future meetings?
qa.a: Chaitanya could mention any possible urgent interruption at the start or ask for a moment, and Pradeep could ask for full attention kindly.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt when he saw Pradeep rush?
qa.a: Chaitanya was probably sorry and a bit embarrassed that his glance looked like boredom.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a glance at a phone read as boredom when it was urgent work, resolved by naming it.

subtype: Looking at the phone versus at the person [Interpreting]
passage:
Monday night.
Gave my first big presentation to the regional managers today. Five minutes in, I saw Anjali, the operations lead, look down at her phone. Then again. Then she typed something. My stomach dropped. I'd spent a week on those slides. I kept going, but my voice got faster and flatter.
Afterwards, I almost walked past her. But I made myself ask. "Anjali, I noticed you on your phone. Was the presentation losing you?"
She looked surprised. "No! I was forwarding your cost slide to the Nagpur team in real time. They've been asking for exactly that." She showed me the message.
I felt stupid. And relieved.
She did add, "I should have said so. Next time, tell me if it bothers you." So I will.
— Divyansh

qa.q: What was Anjali forwarding to the Nagpur team?
qa.a: The cost slide.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when Anjali looked at her phone?
qa.a: Divyansh felt a sinking disappointment, stomach dropping, worried the presentation was losing her, and sped up nervously.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do that was kinder than assuming disrespect?
qa.a: Divyansh asked Anjali directly about the phone instead of walking past her.

qa.q: How did Anjali see her own phone use?
qa.a: As doing a real work task, forwarding the slide, though she admitted she should have said so.

grounding: Shows a young professional reading a colleague's phone use as boredom when it was a work task, and checking kindly.

subtype: Looking at the phone versus at the person [Interpreting]
passage: At the monthly meeting of the milk cooperative in Anand district, Santosh, twenty-five, was explaining the new collection timings to the committee. Parveen, the secretary, kept glancing at her phone, thumb moving fast. Two members exchanged looks. Santosh felt irritation rise. He had worked hard on this plan. Was she even listening? He paused and said, calmly, "Parveen-ji, I notice you're on your phone. Is something urgent? This part needs your approval." Parveen looked up, apologetic. "Sorry, Santosh-bhai. The tanker driver is stuck at the bridge with today's milk. I was arranging another route." Santosh's irritation melted. "Then please sort that first. We'll wait five minutes." She made one more call, put the phone face down and said, "Now, the timings. Go ahead." She approved them with one change. Afterwards a committee member said, "Good that you asked. I thought she didn't care."

qa.q: Where was the tanker driver stuck?
qa.a: At the bridge, with today's milk.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when Parveen kept looking at her phone?
qa.a: He felt irritated and a bit hurt, wondering if she was even listening to the plan he had worked hard on.

qa.q: What did Santosh do that was kinder than assuming disrespect?
qa.a: He named what he noticed calmly, asked if something was urgent, and then gave her time to sort it before continuing.

qa.q: How did the committee member see Parveen's phone use before Santosh asked?
qa.a: The member thought Parveen didn't care about the meeting.

grounding: Shows a young professional noticing a colleague's phone glances, naming the concern and asking instead of assuming disrespect.

subtype: Looking at the phone versus at the person [Interpreting]
passage:
Vera was halfway through her slides on the new delivery routes when she saw Rafael glance at his phone. Then again. Then he typed something under the table.
Her throat tightened. Rafael had pushed back on her plan last week; maybe this was his way of saying it didn't matter. The meeting room in the Lyon office was small, and everyone could see.
She paused at the next slide. "Rafael, I notice you're on your phone. This part affects your team the most, so I'd really like your full attention for the next five minutes. Is something going on?"
Rafael looked up, cheeks pink. "Sorry. The loading dock scanner is down and my night crew keeps messaging me. Give me one minute to hand it to Chloé?"
He stepped out, came back, and put the phone face down on the table.

qa.q: Where was the meeting room?
qa.a: The meeting room was in the Lyon office.

qa.q: What was Vera worried about when Rafael kept looking at his phone?
qa.a: Vera felt hurt and worried that Rafael was dismissing her plan after pushing back last week; she still left room for something urgent and asked.

qa.q: What small step helped here?
qa.a: Naming what she noticed and asking for full attention for five minutes, with an open question, let Rafael explain the scanner problem and hand it off.

qa.q: How did Rafael feel when Vera named the phone use?
qa.a: Rafael seemed embarrassed, with pink cheeks, but the calm question let him explain the urgent problem instead of being blamed for disrespect.

grounding: A colleague's phone glances may mean urgency rather than boredom, and naming the concern and asking for attention is kinder than assuming disrespect.
